column3: The Hebrew says his day without explicitly adding birth.
The Hebrew says Job answered and spoke; BSB says this is what he said.
The Hebrew uses an active verb, said; BSB uses the impersonal passive it was said.
The Hebrew presents darkness as a wish; BSB begins with a wish about what had happened.
The Hebrew says the day’s darknesses terrify it; BSB says overwhelm it.
The Hebrew says the night should not rejoice among the year’s days; BSB says it should not appear among them.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew makes the cursers active; BSB uses a passive curse.
The Hebrew pictures dawn’s eyelids; BSB says the breaking of dawn. Its stars belong to twilight rather than explicitly to morning.
The Hebrew coordinates closing the womb’s doors and hiding trouble; BSB makes hiding sorrow the purpose.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew makes knees the subject of receiving him and describes his suckling actively; BSB uses a passive for nursing.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew describes building ruins for themselves; BSB supplies cities and their present ruined state.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew calls the miscarriage hidden; BSB frames being hidden as a question.
Close to the Hebrew.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew says the slave is free, rather than narrating his being freed.
The Hebrew uses an active giving verb without naming its subject; BSB uses a passive.
The Hebrew says they dig for death more than for hidden treasures; BSB compares their search to searching for hidden treasure.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew continues with to a man without repeating the question or life given, which BSB supplies.
The Hebrew says his sighing comes before his bread; BSB says he sighs when food is put before him.
The Hebrew repeats the root of fear; BSB says the thing he feared.
The Hebrew coordinates trouble coming with the preceding denials; BSB makes it the cause with for.
